chapter.title: Three checks in five minutes

cards.body: Stand in front of the house and ask three quick questions. Do the bills due this year fit inside what you could collect or sell this year? How much of the house really belongs to the bank, compared with you? And is there enough cash in the drawer for the loan payment due next month? Three questions, three divisions, one answer: can this house pay its way this year.

cards.title: Three divisions, one question
cards.body:
Every check on a balance sheet is the same move: take a number the company can pay with, and compare it with a number it must pay. Bigger on the paying side is good. Smaller is a warning.

Check 1 is current assets divided by current liabilities. Current assets are the fast things from chapter 3: cash, stock, bills customers owe. Current liabilities are the debts due within 12 months from chapter 4. If the answer is above 1, the company has more coming in this year than going out. Many people treat 1.5 to 2 as comfortable and below 1 as a flag.

Check 2 is total debt divided by equity. Total debt is every loan, short and long. Equity is the owners' share from chapter 5. The answer tells you how much of the house belongs to lenders for every 1 that belongs to the owners. A result of 1 means lenders and owners have put in about the same. Above 2 means the lenders own most of the house, and a bad year hurts fast.

Check 3 is cash against short-term debt, meaning loans and overdrafts due within 12 months. This one is the strictest. Stock has to be sold before it is money. Customer bills have to be collected. Cash is money today. If cash is smaller than the debt due this year, the company is relying on selling and collecting in time.

You only need the totals. Each check is one division on a phone calculator.

cards.prompt: A company shows current assets of 120 and current liabilities of 80. What does check 1 say?

options.text: Comfortable: it has 1.5 of fast assets for every 1 due within the year
A warning: 80 of bills is a large amount to owe
Can't tell until you know this year's profit

whyNot.b: That's reading the size of the number, not the comparison: 80 only matters next to the 120 that can pay it.
whyNot.c: That's the income statement, not the balance sheet: profit over a year is not what you have on hand to pay bills today.

cards.reteach: Check 1 is a division, not a size judgement. Fast assets 120 divided by bills due soon 80 gives 1.5. Above 1 means more can be paid than is due, and 1.5 sits in the range most people call comfortable.

cards.title: A furniture shop on 31 March
cards.body:
The shop's balance sheet shows current assets of 300: cash 50, stock 150, customer bills 100. Current liabilities are 250, of which 90 is a bank loan due within the year. Total debt is 400 and equity is 200.

Check 1: 300 divided by 250 is 1.2. It passes, but not by much. Check 2: 400 divided by 200 is 2. Lenders have put in twice what the owners have. Check 3: cash 50 against a 90 loan due soon. It fails. The shop cannot pay that loan from cash. It needs to sell sofas or collect from customers first.

One sentence: the shop can cover this year on paper, but it is thin on cash and heavy on borrowing.

cards.title: Why one check is never enough
cards.body:
The shop passed check 1 and failed check 3. That is common, and it is the reason you run all three. Check 1 counts stock and customer bills as if they will turn into money on time. Check 3 refuses to count them. When the two disagree, the gap tells you where the risk sits: in the warehouse, or in the customers who have not paid.

Check 2 answers a different worry. A company can pay this year's bills and still be mostly owned by its lenders. High debt against equity means interest keeps coming whether sales do or not, and lenders, not owners, decide what happens if a payment is missed.

After the three divisions, write one sentence. Name which checks pass, which fail, and what the company is leaning on to close the gap. That sentence is the whole point of this chapter.

cards.prompt: A company shows current assets 500, current liabilities 400, cash 20, short-term loans 150, total debt 600, equity 300. Which sentence applies the three checks correctly?

options.text: It covers this year on paper at 1.25 to 1, but holds only 20 cash against 150 of loans due soon, so it is leaning on selling stock and collecting bills in time.
It is safe, because total assets are bigger than total liabilities and the sheet balances.
It fails check 1, because 400 of current liabilities is far more than 20 of cash.

whyNot.b: That's chapter 1's equation, not a health check: the two sides always balance, so balancing proves nothing about paying bills.
whyNot.c: That's mixing check 1 with check 3: check 1 uses all current assets, 500 against 400, which passes. Cash against short-term debt is check 3.

cards.reteach: Run each division with its own pair of numbers. Check 1: 500 against 400 passes. Check 2: 600 against 300 means lenders have put in twice the owners' share. Check 3: 20 cash against 150 due soon fails. The sentence names all three and says what fills the gap.

cards.body: The common mistake is to stop at check 1 and treat stock and unpaid customer bills as if they were cash. A current ratio of 1.3 looks fine until you notice that 20 of cash sits against 150 of loans due in months. Spot it by always doing check 3 straight after check 1. If the first passes and the third fails, ask what has to be sold or collected, and how fast.

cards.prompt: What do all three checks have in common?

options.text: Each compares something the company can pay with against something it must pay or has borrowed
Each compares this year's figure with last year's to see the trend
Each adds the two sides of the sheet to confirm they match

whyNot.b: That's chapter 2's two-dates comparison, not the health checks: these work on a single day's numbers.
whyNot.c: That's the balancing equation from chapter 1: the sheet always matches, so matching tells you nothing about paying bills.

cards.reteach: Every check is one division: a number that can pay, over a number that is owed. Current assets over current liabilities. Total debt over equity. Cash over short-term debt. Above 1 on the paying side is good, below 1 is a flag.

cards.body: Open any listed company's latest annual report on your phone, find the balance sheet page, and do the three divisions on your calculator. Write one sentence on whether it can pay this year.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now run three divisions on any balance sheet and say in one sentence whether the company can pay its bills this year.
